reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: Classically a fracture of the distal radius within a few centimetres of the wrist with dorsal displacement and angulation, producing the 'dinner-fork' deformity
Typically caused by a fall onto the outstretched hand in an older, osteoporotic patient; its occurrence should prompt bone-health assessment
Radiographs show dorsal tilt, radial shortening, and often an associated ulnar styloid fracture; the degree of intra-articular involvement guides management
Undisplaced or minimally displaced fractures are treated with a cast; displaced fractures usually require closed reduction and immobilisation, checking that radial length and volar tilt are restored
Unstable, markedly comminuted, or intra-articular fractures often need surgical fixation such as a volar locking plate or K-wires to maintain alignment
Median nerve symptoms (acute carpal tunnel) can arise from swelling or displacement and must be sought before and after reduction
Watch for later complications including malunion, extensor pollicis longus tendon rupture, stiffness, and complex regional pain syndrome
Early finger, elbow, and shoulder mobilisation during cast treatment helps prevent stiffness and disuse
reference.pathophysiology: A Colles' fracture occurs when a fall onto the dorsiflexed, outstretched hand transmits force through the distal radius, which fails in its metaphyseal cancellous bone. Osteoporosis lowers the threshold for injury, explaining its predominance in postmenopausal women and older adults. The distal fragment tilts and displaces dorsally and radially and impacts proximally, shortening the radius and disrupting the normal volar tilt and radial inclination of the articular surface. Associated soft-tissue swelling or bony displacement may compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, and disruption of the distal radioulnar joint or triangular fibrocartilage can affect forearm rotation.
additionalDifferentials: Smith's fracture (volar displacement) and Barton's fracture (intra-articular shear)
Distal radial physeal injury in adolescents
additionalInvestigations: Posteroanterior and lateral wrist radiographs to assess dorsal tilt, radial length and inclination, and articular involvement
CT for complex intra-articular or comminuted patterns to plan fixation
Post-reduction radiographs to confirm and monitor alignment
Assessment for osteoporosis and secondary fracture prevention in older patients
Clinical assessment of median nerve function before and after reduction
redFlags: Progressive median nerve symptoms indicating acute carpal tunnel syndrome requiring urgent decompression or reduction
Marked deformity with vascular compromise of the hand
Fracture from trivial trauma signalling significant underlying osteoporosis
reference.prognosis: Most stable distal radial fractures unite and recover good function with appropriate reduction and rehabilitation, but malunion with residual dorsal tilt and radial shortening can leave weakness, reduced grip, and cosmetic deformity, and intra-articular incongruity predisposes to post-traumatic arthritis.
pitfalls: Accepting a poor reduction with persistent dorsal tilt or radial shortening, leading to symptomatic malunion
Failing to recognise or monitor acute median nerve compression
Immobilising the wrist in excessive flexion (Cotton-Loder position), which risks stiffness and nerve compression
Neglecting finger and shoulder movement during cast treatment, causing stiffness and complex regional pain syndrome
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
